Two small things that change how all your later code looks.

## Packages

Base R ships with a few thousand functions. Everything else lives in
**packages** other people wrote and published. Using one is 2 steps, and people
mix them up:

| Step | Command | How often |
|---|---|---|
| Install: get it onto your disk | `install.packages("dplyr")` | once, ever |
| Load: make it available now | `library(dplyr)` | every session |

Installing is like buying a book. Loading is like taking it off the shelf. You
buy once; you take it off the shelf every time you want to read it.

::: {.callout-important}
## This browser does one thing your own R will not
This page has already loaded `dplyr` for you before you ran anything. Your own
RStudio will **not**. There, every script starts with its `library()` calls, and
a script that forgets them fails with `could not find function`.

So the `library(dplyr)` line below is a no-op here and essential there. Type it
anyway. It is the habit that matters, and a missing `library()` is a common
reason a script that worked yesterday fails today.
:::

```{webr}
library(dplyr)

# Now dplyr's functions exist by name
glimpse(mtcars)
```

`install.packages()` goes in your **console**, never in a script.

A script that reinstalls its packages every run takes 4 minutes to do 2 seconds
of work. On a machine with no internet it fails outright.

## The pipe

Read this and try to say what it does:

```{webr}
round(sqrt(mean(c(4, 9, 16, 25, 36))), 2)
```

You had to read it inside out: the innermost bracket happens first. That is the
opposite of the order you would describe the work in.

`|>` is the **native pipe**. It takes the thing on its left and makes it the
first argument of the function on its right. Same answer, read left to right:

```{webr}
c(4, 9, 16, 25, 36) |>
  mean() |>
  sqrt() |>
  round(2)
```

"Take these numbers, average them, square-root that, round to two places."
That sentence and that code are now in the same order.

::: {.callout-note}
## Typing it
RStudio has a shortcut: <kbd>Ctrl</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>M</kbd> on
Windows and Linux, <kbd>Cmd</kbd>+<kbd>Shift</kbd>+<kbd>M</kbd> on macOS. By
default it inserts the *other* pipe, `%>%`. Turn on the native one in
**Tools → Global Options → Code → Use native pipe operator**.

You will meet `%>%` in older code and older books. It behaves almost
identically. We use `|>` because it is part of R itself and needs no package.
:::

## Why this matters more than it looks

An analysis is a sequence: start with data, keep some rows, add a column, group
it, summarise it. Written with nested brackets, that sequence is written
backwards and is very hard to edit. Written with pipes it is a list of steps you
can add to, comment out, or reorder.

```{webr}
library(dplyr)

# A five-step analysis that still reads like a sentence
mtcars |>
  filter(cyl == 4) |>
  mutate(kpl = mpg * 0.425) |>
  select(mpg, kpl, wt) |>
  arrange(desc(kpl)) |>
  head(3)
```

Comment out any one line with a `#` and the rest still runs. That is the real
payoff, and it is why the next primer is entirely pipes.

## A pipe is not magic

It only ever does one thing: put the left side into the **first** argument slot
on the right. These two are identical:

```{webr}
c(1, 4, 9) |> sum()
sum(c(1, 4, 9))
```

If a function needs the piped value somewhere other than first, the pipe cannot
help you, and you write the call normally. That is uncommon in the tidyverse,
because tidyverse functions are designed to take the data first for exactly
this reason.

## Exercises

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 1: rewrite with a pipe"}
**Time:** 5 minutes

Seven monthly case counts: 12, 19, 7, 25, 14, 31, 9.

Compute the square root of their mean, rounded to 2 decimal places — and write
it as a **pipeline**, not as nested brackets.

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe
cases <- c(12, 19, 7, 25, 14, 31, 9)

______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe
#| solution: true
cases <- c(12, 19, 7, 25, 14, 31, 9)

cases |>
  mean() |>
  sqrt() |>
  round(2)
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_pipe
#| check: true
# The pipe IS the lesson here: the value 4.09 is obtainable without one, so the
# value alone cannot show the lesson was learnt. This is the one check on this
# page that reads your code rather than your answer.
# fixed = TRUE is load-bearing: as a regex, "|>" means "empty string or >",
# and empty string matches everything, so the check would always pass.
used_pipe    <- grepl("|>", .user_code, fixed = TRUE)
used_magrittr <- grepl("%>%", .user_code, fixed = TRUE)
right_answer <- isTRUE(all.equal(as.numeric(.result), 4.09))

if (right_answer && used_pipe) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct — 4.09, and it reads left to right.")
} else if (right_answer && used_magrittr) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right answer, but that is the magrittr pipe %>%. Use the native |>, which we use throughout this course.")
} else if (right_answer) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Right answer, but rewrite it with |> so it reads in the order the work happens.")
} else if (is.numeric(.result) && length(.result) == 1) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Wrong number. Three steps in this order: mean of the cases, then sqrt of that, then round to 2.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Start with cases, then pipe into mean(), then sqrt(), then round(2).")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_pipe"}
Start with `cases`, then `|> mean()`, then `|> sqrt()`, then `|> round(2)`. Put
each step on its own line; the pipe at the end of a line tells R to keep
reading.
:::
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Exercise 2: install or load?"}
**Time:** 2 minutes

You open RStudio on Monday morning. You installed `ggplot2` last week. You now
want to use it in today's script.

Which single line belongs at the top of that script?

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_load
# Replace the blank with the answer, as a piece of text in quotation marks:
# either "install.packages(\"ggplot2\")" or "library(ggplot2)"

answer <- ______
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_load
#| solution: true
answer <- "library(ggplot2)"
```

```{webr}
#| exercise: ex_load
#| check: true
given <- if (is.character(.result) && length(.result) == 1) .result else ""
if (grepl("library", given, fixed = TRUE) && !grepl("install", given, fixed = TRUE)) {
  list(correct = TRUE, message = "Correct. It is already on disk; you just need it off the shelf. library() belongs in the script, every time.")
} else if (grepl("install", given, fixed = TRUE)) {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Installing is a once-ever job and belongs in the console, not the script. A script that reinstalls every run is slow, and fails with no internet.")
} else {
  list(correct = FALSE, message = "Put one of the two lines in quotation marks, as text. For example: answer <- \"library(ggplot2)\"")
}
```

::: {.hint exercise="ex_load"}
You bought the book last week. What do you do this morning — buy it again, or
take it off the shelf?
:::
:::

## What you should now be able to do

- Tell installing a package from loading one, and say where each belongs.
- Start every script with its `library()` calls, even though this browser does
  not make you.
- Read and write a `|>` pipeline, and explain why it reads better than nested
  brackets.
- Recognise `%>%` in other people's code as the older equivalent.
